details:
ATLAS is an interactive planetary exploration platform designed to identify and compare locations on Earth that resemble the surface environments of the Moon and Mars. Through satellite imagery, topographic visualization, geographic coordinate selection, and 3D terrain comparison, the platform allows users to explore terrestrial analog sites and investigate their similarities and differences with extraterrestrial landscapes. By integrating planetary datasets, geospatial analysis, and logistical considerations, ATLAS also aims to aid the preliminary assessment of Earth analog sites where teams can rehearse missions to potential landing sites and base locations. It makes planetary exploration more accessible by bringing scientific comparisons, geographical information, and practical site considerations into one interactive platform.

What does it do, and what benefits does it offer?

  • Explore planetary environments: Navigate interactive representations of Earth, the Moon, and Mars.
  • Discover terrestrial analogs: Explore locations on Earth that share geological and environmental characteristics with extraterrestrial landscapes.
  • Compare terrain: Examine satellite imagery, topography, and 3D terrain models for the measured pairs to investigate similarities and differences.
  • Investigate locations: Select geographic coordinates to explore potential analog sites beyond the curated examples.
  • Assess logistical considerations: Examine factors such as proximity to towns, airports, and other accessible infrastructure when evaluating terrestrial analog locations.
  • Support mission preparation: show which Earth sites match a Moon or Mars site in which ways, and where they stop matching, so teams can choose where to test equipment and train crews

What is its intended impact?

ATLAS aims to bridge terrestrial research and planetary exploration by making Earth-based analog studies more accessible and useful for mission preparation. By combining environmental comparisons with geographical and logistical information, the platform hopes to support researchers, educators, and mission planners in identifying potential analog environments, testing exploration strategies, and preparing for future lunar and Martian missions.

What tools and technologies were used?

The platform combines web development, scientific programming, and publicly available planetary datasets:

  • HTML, CSS, and JavaScript – Website development and interactive features
  • Python and NumPy – Scientific calculations and data processing
  • Rasterio and PyProj – Geospatial processing and coordinate transformations
  • Leaflet – Interactive mapping
  • NASA LOLA and MOLA datasets – Lunar and Martian elevation data
  • NASA GIBS – Satellite imagery
  • GitHub Pages – Website hosting and deployment
  • Copernicus DEM (ESA): Earth elevation, the Earth side of every terrain measure
  • MODIS land surface temperature: measured temperature at each Earth site
  • NASA POWER: climate (air temperature, wind, rain)
  • NASA Trek and USGS Astrogeology: Moon and Mars imagery and maps
  • Microsoft Planetary Computer: access to the Copernicus DEM and MODIS
  • Mapzen Terrain Tiles: elevation for testing any place
  • Natural Earth: towns and airports for logistics

How is the project creative?

ATLAS transforms familiar terrestrial landscapes into a gateway for understanding other planetary worlds. Rather than relying solely on visual resemblance, it combines measurable terrain characteristics, geographic exploration, and 3D visualization to provide meaningful comparisons. Its integration of logistical considerations also extends its purpose beyond scientific visualization, connecting terrestrial analog research with the practical challenges of planning future space missions.

What factors did the team consider?

  • Scientific accuracy: Using credible research and planetary datasets.
  • Terrain and geology: Evaluating elevation, slope, roughness, and geological characteristics.
  • Environmental conditions: Considering temperature, water and ice, dust, and other relevant factors.
  • Data availability: Accounting for differences in spatial resolution and dataset coverage.
  • Logistical accessibility: Considering straight-line distance to the nearest town and airport.
  • Practical applications: Recognizing how terrestrial analogs can support equipment testing, astronaut training, and future mission preparation.
  • Limitations: Acknowledging that Earth cannot perfectly replicate the environmental conditions of the Moon and Mars.
